newsitem.title: FRANCE: French public audit due in parliament next Monday.
newsitem.headline: French public audit due in parliament next Monday.

text.p: An audit of public finances requested by France's new leftist government will be unveiled next Monday at a meeting of the National Assembly's finance commission, parliament said on Tuesday.

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin ordered the audit to evaluate the state of public finances shortly after taking power six weeks ago when the left defeated the rightist government in a June 1 parliamentary election.
Jospin had said an audit was required before he could make decisions on fulfilling potentially costly campaign promises.

Government sources have said they expect the audit to show the 1997 deficit is running at between 3.5 percent and 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, above the three percent level for France to qualify for European economic and monetary union from 1999.
But officials have said they expect to present a draft 1998 budget in September which respects the three percent criterion, thus showing that the trend is in the right direction.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac said on Monday that this year's public deficit was running at about 3.5 percent of GDP but insisted France could achieve the Maastricht Treaty target of three percent if it held down spending.
Asked about Chirac's statement following a meeting of Jospin's main economic team on Tuesday, Finance Minister Dominique Strauss Kahn declined to comment.
"I am waiting to see the results (of the audit)," he said.

The audit findings will be presented to the assembly committee at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Monday by Jacques Bonnet and Philippe Nasse, senior officials on the government accounting board, parliamentary aides said.
Strauss-Kahn and Secretary of State for Budget Christian Sautter will testify before the same assembly panel at 3 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Monday, the aides said.
Jospin held two and a half hours of talks on Tuesday with Strauss-Kahn, Sautter and Employment and Solidarity Minister Martine Aubry in what aides called an ordinary working session.
